<reason>Both sides were sharp, well-grounded, and format-compliant, but B built the cleaner path on the motion's actual verb: "preferable." B's core burden — that PRO proved the floor must be publicly guaranteed, not that one payer beats many work-linked payers with a backstop — was pressed from B1.3 through the unfalsifiability Q1 to B4.2 ("the motion asks for single-payer, not portability") and never squarely defeated; A's claim that Germany "sits on our side" was an overreach B caught cleanly. On the delivery clash, A's democratic-accountability mechanism was empirically undercut by B4.4 (Canada's queues visible and embarrassing for decades, still there), and A's closing simply re-asserted "visible queues pressure budgets" without answering it. B also won the recession exchange with the marginal-backfill vs. total-revenue-collapse distinction. A had genuinely live unrefuted routes (administrative waste, job lock) but abandoned them in the closing to fight on B's strongest ground. B's clipped Rebuttal 2 and ignored efficiency/freedom pillars keep the margin modest.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Germany exchange: A's concession-capture in A2.1 ("Germany unties access, so it's our side") was caught by B2.1's redefinition charge and converted into B4.2's decisive framing — if a work-linked multi-payer system passes PRO's own floor test, single-payer is unnecessary rather than preferable. Runner-up: B4.4's "visibility has been tested for decades and the queues remain," which dismantled A's accountability mechanism and went unanswered in A's closing.</best_rebuttal>
